title: `trace`: actually seeing the scheduler and the latency

videos.script: Lesson 12's CPU profile answers one question. Where does the program spend its time on a processor? It has nothing to say about the time a goroutine spends waiting. {{record}} This lesson records an execution trace instead. The runtime writes down every moment a goroutine starts, stops, blocks and wakes, each with a timestamp in nanoseconds. Two calls in your program turn it on, or one flag to go test. {{timeline}} Then you read it. go tool trace draws every processor and every goroutine on one timeline. It can also turn the waiting into profiles of its own. {{wait}} The program you trace counts the hits log with four workers. One version shares a mutex badly. Its CPU time looks like a single worker's, and nothing in a CPU profile says why. The trace shows four goroutines taking turns at one lock. {{flight}} Last, the flight recorder. It keeps the most recent trace in memory and writes it out only when something is slow. So a stall that happens once an hour can explain itself.
